question.value: Can high-sensitivity thermal infrared observations with JWST/MIRI detect a sub-Jupiter mass planet responsible for the ring-like structures and gaps in the young debris disk around TWA 7?

evidence.quote: We have used the unprecedented sensitivity of JWST/MIRI [9,10] in the thermal IR to search for such planets in the disk of the ~6.4 Myr old star TWA 7.

We unambiguously detected a source 1.5” from the star, that is best interpreted as a cold, sub-Jupiter mass planet. Its estimated mass (~ 0.3 M J ) and position (~ 52 au, de-projected) can thoroughly account for the main disk structures.
ALMA data were collected during the 2015.1.01015.S program (PI Bayo).
This paper makes use of ALMA data ADS/JAO.ALMA#2015.1.01015.S.
Its location in the MIRI image is consistent with that of a bright source in ALMA band 7 (346 GHz) data from 2016 [20]

analysis_steps.goal: Reduce JWST/MIRI coronagraphic images and extract photometry and astrometry of detected sources

method.value: Retrieve Level 1 data from MAST, process with JWST pipeline v1.14.0, subtract background, register to coronagraph center, subtract stellar diffraction using linear combination and PCA of 9 SGD reference star frames, simulate PSF with WebbPSF and diffraction code, and extract flux/position via PSF fitting and aperture photometry.

evidence.quote: Level 1 data are retrieved from MAST (Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes), processed with v1.14.0 of the pipeline together with CRDS files 1241.

We tested various algorithms and retained a linear combination (which uses the downhill simplex minimization) of the 9 SGD reference star images, as well as the Principal Component Analysis (PCA), as the two algorithms providing the best detection of CC#1.

Based on these CC#1 PSF models, we extracted the flux and the photometry of the object by minimizing the residuals between the data and the models in a 1.5 λ/D area with 3 free parameters (positions, and flux)

key_parameters.value: Annular optimization region 0.5'' to 3'' (linear combination) and 0.5'' to 5'' with 8 PCA components; 1.5 λ/D photometric extraction area; roll 1 only used for photometry.

evidence.quote: We obtained the best compromise by selecting the annular region between 0.5’’ and 3’’, while the 3 sources were masked with a 1 λ/D patch
We proceeded similarly for the PCA, decreasing to 8 components to build the final image to be subtracted to the data in an annular region from 0.5’’ to 5’’ (point sources not masked).
In the roll 2 image, the PSF is more asymmetrical as the planet is closer to the quadrant edge in comparison to roll 1, so we decided to consider only roll 1 data for the photometric analysis.

assumptions.value: Flat field correction is skipped as inappropriate for the MIRI coronagraph.

evidence.quote: We skipped the Flat Field correction which is not appropriate for the MIRI coronagraph [21].

fitting.value: Downhill simplex algorithm or Nelder-Mead algorithm with 3 free parameters (positions and flux) in a 1.5 λ/D area.

evidence.quote: we extracted the flux and the photometry of the object by minimizing the residuals between the data and the models in a 1.5 λ/D area with 3 free parameters (positions, and flux) and using either a downhill simplex algorithm or the NelderMead algorithm [40].

validation.value: Compared two independent PSF simulation codes (yielding consistent transmissions of 0.66 and 0.62 in roll 1), checked alternate annular region (2-3''), and averaged across calibrated/uncalibrated files and PSF/aperture photometry.

evidence.quote: The two approaches give similar transmissions: 0.66 and 0.62 in roll 1 and 0.31 and 0.28 in roll 2.

We averaged the values of the different methods (calibrated files and contrast, aperture and PSF model for the photometric extraction) while the error bar is built from the extreme values ((max-min)/2) for being conservative.

assumptions.value: Evaluated upper limit assuming CC#1 is an unresolved point source that had not moved between 2016 and 2024.

analysis_steps.goal: Fit astrometry and morphology of the bright ALMA East source and compare with MIRI East source

method.value: Fit a point-source model in the visibility domain to each of the 3 ALMA epochs using MCMC (emcee) to obtain astrometry, fit a 2D Gaussian to the combined image to measure integrated flux and size, and translate the ALMA position to the 2024 MIRI epoch using Gaia DR3 stellar proper motion.

evidence.quote: we first measure its RA and Dec in each of the 3 epochs of observations by fitting a point source model with a flux density, RA offset and Dec offset from phase center to the visibility data. We did this using MCMC through the emcee package
To investigate this further, we fit a 2D Gaussian to the combined image, finding best fit FWHMs of 0.35”x0.26” with a PA of 101 degrees, and a spatially integrated flux of 4.0+/-0.4 mJy.
We can therefore translate the ALMA galaxy position (fixed in time, from Supplementary Information Table 1) into an offset from the (Gaia DR3-predicted) position of the TWA 7 star at the MIRI epoch

key_parameters.value: ALMA astrometric systematic error of 5% of the beam size (9 mas for combined observation) added in quadrature to statistical MCMC uncertainties.

evidence.quote: We then once again quadratically add the expected ALMA astrometric systematic (5% of the beam of the combined observation, i.e. 9 mas) to the statistical uncertainty, leading to the final combined ALMA coordinate for the East source.

assumptions.value: The East source is extragalactic and stationary between the 2016 ALMA and 2024 MIRI epochs.

evidence.quote: Assuming the source to be extragalactic, we expect its position not to change between the ALMA and MIRI epochs.

fitting.value: MCMC via emcee with uniform, uninformative priors on flux density, RA offset, and Dec offset in visibility space; 2D Gaussian fit in image plane.

evidence.quote: We did this using MCMC through the emcee package, with uniform, uninformative priors on each of the fitted parameters.
To investigate this further, we fit a 2D Gaussian to the combined image

validation.value: Checked consistency of RA and Dec across the three individual ALMA epochs and inspected residual visibilities/images after model subtraction.

evidence.quote: The resulting RA and Dec (Supplementary Information Table 1) of the East source is consistent across the three ALMA epochs
As shown by imaging the residual visibilities, this is because the source is extended, with extended emission clearly present in each residual image after point source subtraction.

findings_qualitative.value: An unambiguous point source (CC#1 / TWA 7 b) is detected at ~1.5'' North-West of TWA 7 (~51 au projected, ~52 au de-projected) in JWST/MIRI F1140C images, lying directly on the narrow R2 debris ring within an azimuthal underdensity.

evidence.quote: We unambiguously detected a source 1.5” from the star, that is best interpreted as a cold, sub-Jupiter mass planet. Its estimated mass (~ 0.3 M J ) and position (~ 52 au, de-projected) can thoroughly account for the main disk structures.
The observed source is located right on the R2 narrow ring, and, moreover, within a region identified as underdense compared to the rest of the ring by [17] (Figure 3a).

findings_qualitative.value: The spatially resolved MIRI East source (~6.7'' East of TWA 7) is firmly associated with the bright, extended background galaxy detected in archival 2016 ALMA Band 7 observations once TWA 7's proper motion is accounted for.

evidence.quote: We find the offsets to be entirely consistent with one another within the uncertainties, and therefore firmly associate the MIRI East source to the background galaxy detected by ALMA.

findings_qualitative.value: A super-solar metallicity is required by the HADES atmospheric model fits for TWA 7 b.

evidence.quote: A metallicity range above solar is required. Additional data will be necessary to further constrain this parameter.

claims.hypothesis: The source detected ~6.7'' East of TWA 7 in JWST/MIRI F1140C images is the stationary background galaxy previously detected in 2016 ALMA Band 7 data.
claims.experiment: Fit point-source astrometry to three epochs of 2016 ALMA Band 7 visibilities using MCMC (emcee), translate the position to the 2024 MIRI epoch using Gaia DR3 proper motion of TWA 7, and compare with the MIRI East source offset.
claims.result: The predicted stellocentric offset at the MIRI epoch (+6.790 ± 0.015'', +0.002 ± 0.011'') is consistent within uncertainties with the measured MIRI Gal BKG offset (6.74 ± 0.04'', -0.05 ± 0.04'').
claims.finding: The MIRI East source is firmly identified as the background galaxy detected by ALMA.

claims.hypothesis: The candidate companion CC#1 at ~1.5'' North-West of TWA 7 is a background galaxy or a solar system object rather than a bound planet.
claims.experiment: Check for proper motion across two 2-hour MIRI exposures against solar system ephemerides, re-image combined ALMA Band 7 data to place a 3-sigma upper limit at CC#1's position, and compute background galaxy contamination probability using SWIRE templates and GOODS luminosity functions.
claims.result: CC#1 shows proper motion < 0.05''/hr (excluding solar system bodies and Planet Nine), is undetected in ALMA Band 7 (< 76 μJy at 3-sigma) and VLT/SPHERE, yielding a ~0.34% (+0.22/-0.14%) probability of being a background galaxy within 1.5''.
claims.finding: A solar system origin is excluded and a background galaxy origin has very low likelihood (~0.34%).

evidence.quote: Based on the constraints from the planetary ephemeris [26] and the predictions of the orbit of Planet Nine [27], a solar system origin for CC#1 can be excluded definitely.

evidence.loc: Methods, 2. Estimation of the probability for an intermediate-redshift galaxy
evidence.quote: Hence in a radius of 1.5” around TWA7, the probability to have such a galaxy is about 0.34% (+0.22/-0.14%).

claims.hypothesis: CC#1 is a cold, sub-Jovian planet whose mass and orbit explain both the observed photometry/upper limits and the R2 ring and gap structures in the TWA 7 debris disk.
claims.experiment: Fit the JWST F1140C flux and VLT/SPHERE H2/H3 upper limits with HADES cloudy atmospheric/evolutionary models and run symplectic N-body simulations (swift_rmvs3) of a 0.34 M_J planet at 52 au interacting with a planetesimal disk over 6 Myr.
claims.result: Atmospheric and evolutionary models yield Teff = 316 +19/-23 K and mass = 0.34 ± 0.06 M_J (~0.3 M_J), and N-body simulations reproduce a narrow resonant ring at 52 au surrounded by gaps and an azimuthal underdensity centered on the planet.
claims.finding: CC#1 is best interpreted as a ~0.3 M_J, ~320 K planet (TWA 7 b) at ~52 au that sculpts the R2 debris ring and surrounding gaps.

evidence.quote: The low likelihood of a background galaxy, the successful fit of the MIRI flux and SPHERE upper limits by a 0.3 M J planet spectrum, and the fact that a ~0.3 M J planet at the observed position would naturally explain the structure of the R2 ring, its underdensity at the planet’s position, and the gaps, provide compelling evidence supporting a planetary origin for the observed source.
The mass found is 0.34 +/- 0.06 M J (considering errors from the MCMC only).

why_this_data.value: JWST/MIRI provides unprecedented thermal-IR sensitivity to sub-Jovian planets around the young, nearly pole-on three-ring debris disk of TWA 7; archival ALMA Band 7 data are reanalysed to test for a sub-mm counterpart to CC#1 and verify the nature of the East source.

evidence.quote: We have used the unprecedented sensitivity of JWST/MIRI [9,10] in the thermal IR to search for such planets in the disk of the ~6.4 Myr old star TWA 7. With its pole-on orientation, this three-ring debris disk is indeed ideally suited for such a detection.
We reanalysed archival ALMA data on TWA 7 from project 2015.1.01095 to search for any counterpart for CC#1 and to establish the nature of the East source detected in the MIRI images.

why_this_method.value: Used tclean mosaic mode to combine ALMA observations with different phase centers; used natural weighting to maximize point-source sensitivity at CC#1's location and Briggs 0.5 as a compromise between resolution and sensitivity; used only JWST roll 1 for photometry because CC#1 is closer to the 4QPM transition edge in roll 2.

evidence.quote: We repeated the same imaging process also on the combined visibility datasets, but using the tclean mosaic mode to account for the different phase centers of the different observations

To maximize point source sensitivity at the expense of angular resolution, we also use the same method to create a separate image with natural weighting, which has an RMS of 21 μJy/beam for a beam size of 0.29”x0.24”.
In the roll 2 image, the PSF is more asymmetrical as the planet is closer to the quadrant edge in comparison to roll 1, so we decided to consider only roll 1 data for the photometric analysis.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Solar system object (including distant dwarf planets or hypothetical Planet Nine) considered and rejected based on lack of proper motion (< 0.05''/hr) and ephemeris constraints.

evidence.quote: The first origin one can consider is a solar system object.
Based on the constraints from the planetary ephemeris [26] and the predictions of the orbit of Planet Nine [27], a solar system origin for CC#1 can be excluded definitely.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Intermediate-redshift starburst or AGN background galaxy considered and found to have a low probability (~0.34% within 1.5'').

evidence.quote: The second possible origin is a background galaxy.

Using such galaxy templates at various redshifts and published galaxy counts in JWST fields of view, we estimated that the probability of finding one such galaxy in a 1.5” radius region centered on TWA 7 is ~0.34% (see details in Methods).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Target Acquisition (TA) images for JWST contrast calibration were tested and rejected due to broad TA filter bandwidth (~8-18 μm), spectral type mismatch, and disk emission beyond 15 μm.

evidence.quote: The method using TA shows some net discrepancies, likely because the TA filter is very broad (~8-18μm) while the targets have different spectral types (M3 for TWA7 and for K0/K5 for the commissioning targets). Beside, the disk emission of TWA 7 should also start to kick off beyond 15 μm. As a result, we did not use the TA method in the following.

limitations_admitted.value: No second-epoch data are available yet to test whether CC#1 shares common proper motion with TWA 7.

evidence.quote: No data is available to test whether this third source shares a common proper motion with the star.

limitations_admitted.value: The extended TWA 7 debris disk is interferometrically filtered out in the high-resolution ALMA images, and its SNR in tapered data is too low to constrain the stellar position directly from disk emission.

evidence.quote: Note that, as explained in [20], this image does not show the disk because it is too extended and faint; it is then interferometrically ‘filtered out’ by these ALMA configuration observations.
The SNR on the disk is consequently too low to produce sufficiently accurate constraints on the location of the TWA star for comparison with the MIRI data.

limitations_admitted.value: A single 2D Gaussian model leaves significant residuals when subtracted from the ALMA East galaxy image, indicating a more complex core-halo radial surface brightness profile.

evidence.quote: While this model is better at capturing the resolved emission, significant residuals are still present when subtracting this best fit from the image. This suggests a more complex radial surface brightness distribution for this galaxy, with a strongly peaked core and a faint halo of emission.

limitations_admitted.value: N-body dynamical simulations model massless planetesimals rather than dust grains subject to radiation pressure, and planet mass estimates depend on assuming the planet is coeval with the star.

evidence.quote: It however depends on the age of the planet, assumed here to be coeval with its parent star. A younger planet would lead to a smaller mass.
While Figure 3a pictures the grains and Figure 3b the planetesimals, and while some differences may be expected between both distributions due to the radiation pressure acting on the grains

referee_caveats_inferred: Without a second epoch of JWST astrometry to confirm common proper motion, the planetary nature of CC#1 relies on a probabilistic argument against a background galaxy and physical plausibility.

The ALMA non-detection of CC#1 is evaluated at its 2024 MIRI sky position (appropriate for testing a stationary background galaxy), whereas a bound planet on a ~550 yr orbit would have moved slightly between 2016 and 2024.
Note a typo in the Supplementary Information text where the ALMA project code is printed as 2015.1.01095 instead of 2015.1.01015.S (as given in Data Availability and Acknowledgements).
